The manuscript has correctly located the failure: a bare empirical model supplies neither a non-split lift nor a distinguished degree-two class. The decisive obstruction is (iv), with the non-split part of (iii) being essentially the same obstruction in categorical form.

2. Is there a natural subclass on which the data are determined?
There is no convincing subclass defined solely as a class of bare empirical models on which the support suddenly determines the missing data.
The honest named class is:

Operator-realized parity contextuality models with a fixed finite phase group, or more abstractly, empirical models whose compatible measurements form a partial commutative multiplication structure equipped with a central extension by a finite abelian outcome group.

Examples include Pauli, stabilizer, Mermin-square, Mermin-star, and related all-versus-nothing or measurement-based-quantum-computation scenarios.
In such a presentation, products of compatible observables carry phases. The failure of a chosen section of the phase extension to preserve multiplication is a normalized 2-cocycle, and its cohomology class is independent of the chosen section. A nonzero class obstructs a noncontextual value assignment. Okay, Roberts, Bartlett, and Raussendorf prove precisely this kind of H2-criterion for state-independent contextuality. arXiv More recent simplicial and partial-group formulations likewise begin with central-extension or twisting data classified by a degree-two class. arXiv
But this is an enriched contextuality object, not a support-defined subclass in the strict sense. The operator multiplication and its phases are not reconstructible in general from the probability table or possibilistic support. Two physical realizations can present the same combinatorial support while carrying different algebraic realization data.
The three candidate restrictions in the question are insufficient by themselves:


A fixed nerve determines the group in which a class could live, not a preferred element of that group.

but normally does not select one element. It determines a class only in exceptional situations where additional normalization distinguishes a unique invariant element.

Definite verdict
The contextuality crossing is not available from the present manuscript. The manuscript has correctly located the failure: a bare empirical model supplies neither a non-split lift nor a distinguished degree-two class. The decisive obstruction is (iv), with the non-split part of (iii) being essentially the same obstruction in categorical form.
There is a natural enriched class of contextuality models where a degree-two class is determinedâ€”parity and operator-based models carrying multiplication/phase data, equivalently a central extension of compatible observables by a finite phase group. But that construction is not determined by the empirical modelâ€™s support, and the resulting H2-obstruction is already established in the contextuality literature. Moreover, on the overlap where it has been compared with the Abramskyâ€“Mansfieldâ€“Barbosa obstruction, it is no stronger than the degree-one obstruction.
Accordingly, my recommendation is:

Do not spend further effort trying to turn this manuscript into a contextuality paper. Retain and slightly strengthen Section 7 as a boundary theorem, repair its literature coverage, and submit the manuscript at its present mathematical ceiling.

The remaining possibility would be a separate new project, not an extension of the current proof package.

1. Which of (ii)â€“(iv) is the real obstacle?
The real obstacle is (iv)
A finite abelian band can always be imposed by conventionâ€”for example, one could work uniformly with Z/2Z, or with a coefficient group associated with some externally specified outcome algebra. That does not make the choice intrinsically meaningful, but it makes (ii) technically cheap.
Similarly, a bare support sheaf has the canonical split lift
Disc(aSeâ€‹)Ã—BA,
so some answer to (iii) is always available. The manuscript proves that every component of this lift is neutral. It also proves that the AMB class is differently indexed: by a supported local section rather than by a global component section. 
The problem begins when â€œan A-banded prestackâ€ is replaced by â€œa non-split A-banded prestack carrying a contextually meaningful class.â€ Specifying such a lift is, up to the usual equivalence, already specifying the relevant H2-data. Thus the non-split part of (iii) and item (iv) are two descriptions of the same missing input.
The manuscript itself makes this unusually clear: Theorem 4.2 starts from prescribed maps
Ï•Î»â€‹:H2â€‹(N,Z)âŸ¶A
and then constructs the prestack realizing them. It does not extract those maps from F. 
Is the datum underdetermined, or genuinely absent?
Generally it is underdetermined, not nonexistent.
Fix a site, a band A, and a support-like component presheaf. When H2(N;A)î€ =0, there can be many inequivalent non-split lifts with the same underlying component data. Nothing in the set-valued support distinguishes one class from another. The zero class is the only universally available canonical choice, through the split lift.
There are, however, individual scenarios where a nonzero class is genuinely absent: when the relevant H2(N;A) vanishes, no nonzero constant-band degree-two class of the manuscriptâ€™s type exists. So the exact diagnosis is:
UnderdeterminationÂ wheneverÂ nonzeroÂ classesÂ exist;Â actualÂ absenceÂ whenÂ H2=0.â€‹
The manuscriptâ€™s present wording is therefore mathematically accurate: support supplies none of (ii)â€“(iv), and choosing the canonical split product makes all component classes zero. 
One should not strengthen that to â€œno construction can ever exist.â€ The conclusion supported by the paper is narrower:

The support presheaf does not determine a preferred nonzero class among the possible classes.

That is a non-recovery statement, not an absolute nonexistence statement.

2. Is there a natural subclass on which the data are determined?
There is no convincing subclass defined solely as a class of bare empirical models on which the support suddenly determines the missing data.
The honest named class is:

Operator-realized parity contextuality models with a fixed finite phase group, or more abstractly, empirical models whose compatible measurements form a partial commutative multiplication structure equipped with a central extension by a finite abelian outcome group.

Examples include Pauli, stabilizer, Mermin-square, Mermin-star, and related all-versus-nothing or measurement-based-quantum-computation scenarios.
In such a presentation, products of compatible observables carry phases. The failure of a chosen section of the phase extension to preserve multiplication is a normalized 2-cocycle, and its cohomology class is independent of the chosen section. A nonzero class obstructs a noncontextual value assignment. Okay, Roberts, Bartlett, and Raussendorf prove precisely this kind of H2-criterion for state-independent contextuality. arXiv More recent simplicial and partial-group formulations likewise begin with central-extension or twisting data classified by a degree-two class. arXiv
But this is an enriched contextuality object, not a support-defined subclass in the strict sense. The operator multiplication and its phases are not reconstructible in general from the probability table or possibilistic support. Two physical realizations can present the same combinatorial support while carrying different algebraic realization data.
The three candidate restrictions in the question are insufficient by themselves:


A fixed nerve determines the group in which a class could live, not a preferred element of that group.


A group action restricts a natural class to the invariant subgroup
H2(N;A)G,
but normally does not select one element. It determines a class only in exceptional situations where additional normalization distinguishes a unique invariant element.


Computability of H2â€‹(N,Z) tells one how to evaluate a supplied class; it does not manufacture the class.


So the best named class is operator-realized parity or central-extension contextuality, but it does not give the manuscript a new theorem: that territory is already occupied, and the extra structure lies outside the manuscriptâ€™s empirical-model input.

4. Would a degree-two class see anything the AMB obstruction misses?
The original AMB obstruction is not complete
It is important not to close the direction for the wrong reason. The ordinary AMB degree-one obstruction is not complete for possibilistic contextuality. It gives a sufficient condition, and examples such as Hardy exhibit false positives caused by passage to free abelian combinations. CarÃ¹ also produced a strongly contextual model for which the standard cohomological obstruction fails even under substantial symmetry and connectedness assumptions. arXiv+1
CarÃ¹â€™s later joint-model construction repairs many such failures and gives a complete invariant for the broad class satisfying the cyclic contextuality property, while conjecturing eventual completeness more generally. arXiv
Thus the answer is not that degree one is already universally complete.

The decisive answer

Known AMB-blind phenomena certainly exist. The strongly contextual counterexamples and Hardy-type failures are the relevant phenomena. 6. Can the impossibility itself become a theorem?
Not in the universal form proposed
A theorem saying

â€œNo functor from empirical models to banded prestacks can be natural and produce nonzero degree-two classesâ€

is false or at least indefensible without severe qualifications.
One can enrich the category of models with operator multiplication or central-extension data, and then natural nonzero degree-two classes do exist. Even on bare scenarios, arbitrary functorial conventions can sometimes select classes. The words â€œnatural,â€ â€œempirical-model morphism,â€ â€œcoefficient group,â€ and â€œsite associated to a modelâ€ must all be fixed before a no-go statement has mathematical content.
A genuine but modest no-selection theorem is available
There is an elementary naturality obstruction that can be stated entirely in contextuality and topology terms:

Equivariant no-selection theorem. Suppose an assignment associates to every empirical model e a class
Î˜(e)âˆˆH2(N(Meâ€‹);Aeâ€‹)

This follows immediately by applying naturality to each automorphism of e. It directly answers one of the proposed subclass ideas: symmetry does not generally create a class; it can instead forbid one.
I would put the probability of proving that statement correctly at 98%. Its likely mathematical impact is modest because the core argument is a standard fixed-point observation.
A second precise statement is also available:

The manuscriptâ€™s prescribed-realization theorem can supply examples of this phenomenon. It would still be priced primarily as a consequence of gerbe classification.
I therefore do not recommend recasting the paper around an impossibility theorem. The strongest universal claim is false; the provable restricted claims are correct but too formal to raise the paper materially.

The third field
There is a third field that the manuscript touches:
Finite model theory and constraint satisfaction
Its standard objects are:


finite relational structures;


constraint-satisfaction instances;


partial homomorphisms and locally consistent families of partial solutions;


global homomorphisms;

This is a real contact, not merely a terminological analogy. CSP and structure-isomorphism problems have been formulated through presheaves of local homomorphisms, with cohomological obstructions to extending locally consistent data to global solutions. The standard connecting obstruction for lifting an H0-class remains an H1-class arising from a short exact sequence, just as in the contextuality construction. arXiv
But the same source-side problem recurs. A CSP instance canonically supplies a set-valued presheaf of partial solutions; it does not canonically supply a non-split banded prestack or a distinguished H2-class. The present machinery would again begin only after the crucial semantic construction had been supplied.

the manuscript already contains a technically correct empirical-model boundary;

CSP would require a larger translation before reaching standard objects, and its existing cohomological local-consistency literature would create a new priority audit of its own. Distributed computing is still less promising: there the standard topology is attached to protocol and task complexes, and the manuscript has no construction from those complexes to its non-split lift data.

Final recommendation
The ceiling remains essentially where it was.
The manuscript has a defensible categorical contribution consisting of terminal rigidity, the exact torsor correction, and simultaneous realization of supplied finite-site H2-data. Its own abstract accurately marks the endpoint as a realization theorem that does not transfer to bare empirical models. 
The contextuality section should remain a negative boundary, with one literature repair:

Do not build another theorem into this manuscript in pursuit of the contextuality crossing. Submit it where it stands.

## Instruction Priority

Superpowers skills override default system prompt behavior, but **user instructions always take precedence**:

1. **User's explicit instructions** (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, direct requests) â€” highest priority
2. **Superpowers skills** â€” override default system behavior where they conflict
3. **Default system prompt** â€” lowest priority

If CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or AGENTS.md says "don't use TDD" and a skill says "always use TDD," follow the user's instructions. The user is in control.

## How to Access Skills

**In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and presented to youâ€”follow it directly. Never use the Read tool on skill files.

**In Copilot CLI:** Use the `skill` tool. Skills are auto-discovered from installed plugins. The `skill` tool works the same as Claude Code's `Skill` tool.

**In Gemini CLI:** Skills activate via the `activate_skill` tool. Gemini loads skill metadata at session start and activates the full content on demand.

**In other environments:** Check your platform's documentation for how skills are loaded.

## Platform Adaptation

Skills use Claude Code tool names. Non-CC platforms: see `references/copilot-tools.md` (Copilot CLI), `references/codex-tools.md` (Codex) for tool equivalents. Gemini CLI users get the tool mapping loaded automatically via GEMINI.md.

# Using Skills

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action.** Even a 1% chance a skill might apply means that you should invoke the skill to check. If an invoked skill turns out to be wrong for the situation, you don't need to use it.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOPâ€”you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept â‰  using the skill. Invoke it. |

1. **Process skills first** (brainstorming, debugging) - these determine HOW to approach the task
2. **Implementation skills second** (frontend-design, mcp-builder) - these guide execution

"Let's build X" â†’ brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
"Fix this bug" â†’ debugging first, then domain-specific skills.

**Flexible** (patterns): Adapt principles to context.

The skill itself tells you which.

\section{Boundary with empirical-model obstructions}
\label{sec:empirical-boundary}

Let \(X\) be a finite set of measurements, let \(O_x\) be a finite nonempty
outcome set for each \(x\in X\), and let \(\mathcal M\) be a finite antichain
of contexts covering \(X\).  For a finite empirical model \(e\), write
\[
 S_e(U)=\operatorname{supp}(e_U)
\]
for its support presheaf on the downward-closed context category.  Adjoin a
terminal object \(X\), declare \(\mathcal M\) to cover it, and set
\[
 \widehat S_e(X)=\varprojlim_{U}S_e(U).
\]
Thus \(\widehat S_e(X)\) is the set of compatible supported local
assignments.  Let \(aS_e\) be the associated sheaf on this terminally
augmented context site.

\subsection*{The terminal augmentation}

On the original downward-closed context category, a global assignment is a
compatible family rather than a section over a named terminal context,
because the full measurement set \(X\) need not belong to the measurement
cover.  The augmentation adjoins \(X\) as a bookkeeping object and declares
the maximal contexts to cover it.  Its value is
\[
 \widehat S_e(X)
 =\left\{(s_C)_{C\in\mathcal M}:
 \begin{array}{l}
 s_C\in S_e(C),\\
 s_C|_{C\cap D}=s_D|_{C\cap D}
 \text{ for all }C,D
 \end{array}\right\}.
\]

Because the event sheaf has unique gluing, a compatible family determines a
unique outcome assignment \(s\in\prod_{x\in X}O_x\) whose restriction to
each \(C\) is \(s_C\).  Conversely, any assignment whose restriction lies
in every specified support gives such a family.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contextual-global-set}
 \widehat S_e(X)
 \cong
 \left\{s\in\prod_{x\in X}O_x:
 s|_C\in S_e(C)\ \text{for all }C\in\mathcal M\right\}.
\end{equation}

The plus construction for the cover \(\mathcal M\to X\) produces the same
set.  All members of a matching family agree strictly on intersections, and
the event sheaf supplies their unique outcome assignment.  Thus
\[
 (aS_e)(X)\cong\widehat S_e(X).
\]
Strong contextuality therefore gives an empty set of global component
sections in the canonical support construction, not a nonempty set of
components carrying non-neutral gerbes.

\begin{theorem}[Empirical-model boundary]
\label{thm:empirical-model-boundary}
For every finite empirical model \(e\):
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item compatible supported families, globally supported assignments, global
      sections in the Abramsky--Brandenburger sense, and elements of
      \(\widehat S_e(X)\cong(aS_e)(X)\) are naturally the same set.  Hence
      strong contextuality is absence of a matching family at this
      set-valued level, not matching without amalgamation;
\item for every supplied abelian sheaf \(\mathscr A\),
      \[
      \operatorname{Disc}(aS_e)\times\mathsf B\mathscr A
      \]
      is a canonical split \(\mathscr A\)-banded stack lift of \(aS_e\),
      and every one of its component gerbes is neutral;
\item the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction attached to
      \(s\in S_e(C_0)\) is a relative class
      \[
      \gamma_e(s)\in
      \check H^1(\mathcal M,\mathcal F_{e,\overline C_0}),
      \]
      equivalently a torsor class.  It is not the Giraud \(H^2\)-class of a
      component gerbe.  There can be no construction recovering all such
      classes from a component-section map with component sheaf \(aS_e\):
      for a strongly contextual model the latter map has empty domain
      \((aS_e)(X)=\varnothing\), whereas the AMB classes remain indexed by
      local sections;
\item the homological images and the two-component criterion of
      \Cref{thm:wedge-sphere-two-component-label-loss} apply to an empirical
      model only after a band and a non-split banded prestack lift have been
      supplied as additional data.  They are not invariants of a bare
      empirical model.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The event presheaf
\(\mathcal E(U)=\prod_{x\in U}O_x\) is a sheaf.  A compatible family
\((s_C)_{C\in\mathcal M}\), with \(s_C\in S_e(C)\), therefore glues
uniquely to an assignment \(s\in\prod_{x\in X}O_x\), and its restrictions
lie in the stated supports.  Conversely, restricting such an assignment
gives the compatible family.  The terminal right Kan extension is the same
limit by definition, and the plus construction on the cover
\(\mathcal M\to X\) gives the same set in \((aS_e)(X)\).  This proves (i)
and agrees with the standard support formulation of contextuality
\cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011}.

The four descriptions in (i) fit into a commutative square:
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\{\text{compatible support families}\}
 &\longrightarrow&
\{\text{outcome assignments locally in the support}\}\\
\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\
\widehat S_e(X)&\longrightarrow&(aS_e)(X).
\end{array}
\]
The upper arrow is unique gluing in \(\mathcal E\), the left arrow is the
definition of the inverse limit, and the lower arrow is the plus-construction
map.  Every arrow is a bijection.  No groupoid or band enters this set-level
statement.

The discrete-groupoid functor sends a sheaf of sets to a stack with that
component sheaf and zero automorphism sheaves.  The classifying stack
\(\mathsf B\mathscr A\) has one component and automorphism sheaf
\(\mathscr A\).  Their product is therefore a split banded lift of
\(aS_e\).  In each component, the identity \(\mathscr A\)-torsor is a
global object, so the component gerbe is neutral and its Giraud class is
zero.  This proves (ii).

Objectwise, the product stack has objects
\[
 (s,T),
 \qquad
 s\in(aS_e)(U),\quad
 T\text{ an }\mathscr A|_U\text{-torsor}.
\]
Two objects can be isomorphic only when their first coordinates agree.
Consequently the component sheaf is \(aS_e\).  The automorphism sheaf of
\((s,T)\) is canonically \(\mathscr A|_U\).  For a global component
section \(s\), the object
\[
 (s,\mathscr A)
\]
with the trivial torsor lies globally in the corresponding full component.
This identifies the neutralizing object directly.

Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa apply the free-abelian presheaf
\(\mathcal F_e=\mathbb Z[S_e]\) and a relative kernel presheaf to obtain
the displayed degree-one Cech class
\cite[Sec.~4]{AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012}.  Car\`u identifies this
class with an appropriate torsor trivialized by the measurement cover
\cite[Prop.~6.3]{Caru2017}.  By contrast, the map in
\Cref{prop:standard-component-gerbe-package} is indexed by global sections
of the component sheaf and takes values in derived \(H^2\) of a sheaf band.
If \(e\) is strongly contextual, (i) gives
\((aS_e)(X)=\varnothing\), so every such component-section map has empty
domain.  Local sections \(s\in S_e(C_0)\) can still exist and index AMB
classes.  This degree and indexing mismatch proves (iii).

The mismatch has two independent parts:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 &\text{AMB obstruction}&\text{component-gerbe obstruction}\\ \hline
\text{index}&s\in S_e(C_0)&v\in(aS_e)(X)\\
\text{degree}&\check H^1&H^2\\
\text{object}&\text{relative torsor}&\text{banded gerbe}\\
\text{canonical lift}&\text{relative kernel data}&\text{split stack.}
\end{array}
\]
Changing degree by a formal shift would not repair the indexing difference.
In a strongly contextual model the right-hand index set is empty, while the
left-hand index set can contain many local sections.  When a global support
assignment does exist, the canonical component indexed by it is neutral.
A nonzero degree-two class requires additional lift data in either case.

Finally, the canonical lift in (ii) has zero component classes and zero
homological image subgroups.  A non-split lift, a finite good-cover nerve,
and prescribed maps \(H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A\) are additional inputs to
\Cref{thm:prescribed-component-image-construction}; none is selected by the
support presheaf of a bare empirical model.  This proves (iv).
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Additional data required for the finite-site construction}

To apply the prescribed-realization theorem to an empirical model, one would
have to supply, at minimum:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item a finite intersection site with connected nonempty overlaps and a
      connected nerve;
\item a finite abelian band \(A\);
\item an \(A\)-banded prestack whose component presheaf is related to the
      chosen support data;
\item normalized Cech \(2\)-cocycles, or prescribed maps
      \(H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A\), for its component labels;
\item the terminal-fibre behavior required by the comparison criterion.
\end{enumerate}
The support presheaf supplies none of (ii)--(iv).  It supplies a canonical
answer only after one chooses the split product stack, and that answer sets
every degree-two component class to zero.  No construction established here
maps bare support presheaves to the non-split data used by the wedge
corollary.

One may postulate such lift data for a particular empirical model and then
apply the article's theorems conditionally.  The resulting homological images
belong to that supplied finite presentation and lift, not to the empirical
model alone.  The distinction is the same as in the opening interface: the
paper begins after the site, band, and prestack have been specified.

The theorem concerns possibilistic support.  Probabilistic
noncontextuality asks for a distribution on the global assignment set with
the given marginals, a different extension problem which is not determined
by \(S_e\).  This distinction is independent of the degree mismatch above.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

A stack in groupoids has a sheaf of connected components.  A global section
of that sheaf need not be represented by a global object of the stack, but it
does select a maximal subgerbe.  This is Giraud's component-gerbe construction
\cite[III, Prop.~2.1.5.3]{Giraud1971}.  The component is represented by a
global object precisely when its gerbe is neutral, or equivalently when its
Giraud \(H^2\)-class vanishes.  These classical facts are the starting point
of the article.

Our setting is deliberately finite and presentation-relative.  We fix a site
with terminal object, a presheaf \(F\), an abelian-banded prestack lift
\(\mathfrak P\), and its stackification \(\mathfrak L\).  The connected
components of \(\mathfrak P\) recover \(F\), while those of
\(\mathfrak L\) recover the sheafification \(aF\).  If \(F\) is separated on
the terminal slice and stackification is essentially surjective on the
terminal fibre, a strict matching family without an amalgamation occurs
exactly when \((aF)(a)\) is nonempty and every component gerbe selected by a
section of \((aF)(a)\) is non-neutral.  This is a comparison between a strict
presheaf predicate and standard gerbe theory, not a new classification of
gerbes.

The first paper-specific point is a rigidity statement for a particularly
strong kind of prestack presentation.  Suppose one selects a representative
of every presheaf component and requires those representatives to be stable
under pullback as literal equalities with respect to a split cleavage.  Under
slice separatedness, terminal essential surjectivity then forces the
sheafification unit
\[
 F(a)\longrightarrow(aF)(a)
\]
to be surjective.  Conversely, when \(H^1\) of the band vanishes,
surjectivity makes the Isom torsor between a selected representative and an
arbitrary terminal stack object trivial.  The result is a three-way
equivalence between terminal essential surjectivity, bijectivity of the
terminal sheafification unit, and the sheaf gluing condition at the terminal
object.  The proof in \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} distinguishes the
strict-representative step from the classical \(H^1\)-torsor step.

The second point is an explicit finite-label prestack packaging on one fixed
cover and with one fixed band.  Let \(\mathcal U\) be a finite good cover with
connected nerve \(N\), let \(A\) be a finite abelian group, assume
\(H_1(N,\mathbb Z)=0\), and prescribe a finite family
\[
 \phi_\lambda:H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow A.
\]
The maps, equivalently the corresponding gerbe classes under UCT, are
supplied in advance.  UCT selects the classes in \(H^2(N,A)\), and the
standard Cech construction realizes each class by an \(A\)-banded gerbe
\cite{Breen2006,Moerdijk2002}.  The construction in
\Cref{thm:prescribed-component-image-construction} assembles these gerbes
into one prestack at object level while controlling four features
simultaneously:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item the presheaf and sheaf of component labels;
\item terminal essential surjectivity of stackification;
\item the exact set of neutral and non-neutral labels;
\item the evaluation maps and their image subgroups.
\end{enumerate}
The full construction and all four verifications are part of the article.

There is a coefficient hypothesis which cannot be suppressed.  For an
ordinary nerve to index the Cech cochain complex with one copy of \(A\) per
simplex, every nonempty finite overlap must be connected and the coefficient
trivializations must coherently identify every coefficient group with the
same fixed \(A\) and every restriction map with the identity of \(A\).  On a
disconnected overlap \(U_J\), the section group is \(A^{\pi_0(U_J)}\),
information which the ordinary nerve does not contain.  Thus this is not a
comparison theorem for arbitrary local systems.  We impose the
connected-overlap hypothesis explicitly in
\eqref{eq:connected-overlap-hypothesis}.  The open-star covers used for the
wedge application have contractible nonempty intersections and satisfy it.

We also separate the formal algebra from the realization.  For a class
\(\omega\in H^2(N,A)\), put
\[
 K_\omega=\operatorname{Im}
 \bigl(H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_\omega}A\bigr),
 \qquad Q_\omega=A/K_\omega.
\]
UCT naturality, quotient initiality, character annihilators, and the Ext
kernel are collected in one proposition.  For finitely many component
classes, the two aggregate quotients are
\[
 A/\bigcap_vK_v,
 \qquad A/\sum_vK_v,
\]
and their comparison is the elementary exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow
 \frac{\sum_vK_v}{\bigcap_vK_v}
 \longrightarrow
 A/\bigcap_vK_v
 \longrightarrow
 A/\sum_vK_v
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
No independent information-theoretic claim is made for the cardinalities of
these fibres.

The finite-group endpoint is correspondingly stated as a realization
corollary.  On the all-subdivision open-star basis of a finite model of
\(\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2\), a nonzero finite abelian group \(G\) is
realized as the comparison kernel for two complementary nonzero component
images exactly when
\[
 d(G)\le2\beta
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 G\text{ is not cyclic of prime-power order}.
\]
The proof combines the prescribed-image prestack with the elementary fact
that the indecomposable finite abelian groups are the cyclic prime-power
groups.  It is not a classification attached to an arbitrary space,
presentation, or empirical model.

\subsection*{Inputs, standard steps, and paper-specific steps}

The logical order of the construction is
\[
\begin{array}{c}
(\mathcal C,F,\mathfrak P,\mathscr A)\\
\big\downarrow\text{\scriptsize stackification}\\
\mathfrak L,\ \pi_0(\mathfrak L)\cong aF\\
\big\downarrow\text{\scriptsize pull back over }v\in(aF)(a)\\
\mathfrak G_v,\ [\mathfrak G_v]\in H^2(\mathcal C,\mathscr A)\\
\big\downarrow\text{\scriptsize selected finite presentation and UCT}\\
\operatorname{ev}_{\omega_v}:H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A,\quad
K_v,\quad Q_v.
\end{array}
\]
The first line is supplied data.  The component gerbe in the third line is
Giraud's standard maximal subgerbe over a component section.  Its neutrality
criterion and transport under a banded equivalence are also standard.  The
last line uses standard Cech comparison and UCT after a finite presentation
has been selected.

The article-specific statements concern restrictions and simultaneous
control across this sequence.  The rigidity theorem identifies a strict
representative hypothesis that collapses a possible terminal gluing failure
when \(H^1\) vanishes.  The terminal torsor obstruction shows, without a
representative-rigidity hypothesis, that terminal essential surjectivity on
a neutral component makes the source fibre equivalent to the full
\(\mathscr A\)-torsor groupoid.  Accordingly, the essentially surjective
marked terminal form uses a marking map whose fibre over each neutral label
is an \(H^1\)-torsor, with \(H^0\) as the automorphism group of every object;
it does not identify the terminal prestack classes with the neutral-label
set unless \(H^1\) vanishes.  From supplied gerbe classes, equivalently their
UCT evaluations, the prescribed-realization theorem constructs one prestack
on the fixed cover and fixed band in which the component presheaf, terminal
fibre, neutrality set, and finite family of evaluations are fixed together.
The wedge result is
then a corollary obtained by combining that construction with finite-group
arithmetic.  It is not presented as a separate classification mechanism.

This division also explains the theorem count.  Component-gerbe existence,
neutrality, banded naturality, UCT, duality, subgroup sums and intersections,
and quotient-fibre cardinality are consolidated rather than restated as
independent theorems.  Numbered statements are retained only where they
serve one of three roles:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item record the standard component-gerbe package with its exact Giraud
      antecedent;
\item state a structural obstruction or a paper-specific comparison,
      rigidity, or simultaneous
      realization assertion;
\item isolate an application boundary or the wedge realization endpoint.
\end{enumerate}

There are likewise two distinct uses of cohomology.  The Giraud class
\[
 [\mathfrak G_v]\in H^2(\mathcal C,\mathscr A)
\]
decides neutrality of the full component gerbe.  After a finite connected
good-cover presentation with constant coefficient group \(A\) is fixed, its
image under
\[
 H^2(N,A)\longrightarrow
 \operatorname{Hom}(H_2(N,\mathbb Z),A)
\]
measures only evaluation on integral \(2\)-cycles.  A nonzero Ext class can
be invisible to this map.  The homological image is therefore a quotient
construction applied to a supplied gerbe class, not a complete obstruction
theory for neutrality.

\subsection*{Scope and relation to the companion manuscript}

The lift data in this article are supplied.  They are not constructed from
teams, logical models, or empirical probability tables.  A bare empirical
model has a canonical split stack lift whose component gerbes are neutral.
The Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative Cech
\(H^1\)-torsor class indexed by a local section
\cite{AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,Caru2017}.  The empty-domain argument
in \Cref{thm:empirical-model-boundary} prevents a universal recovery of those
classes from a global-component-section map.

The companion manuscript
\cite{MaZhang2026ConditionalGluingFailure} uses meet-semilattice sites.  The
overlap with the present pullback-site treatment is as follows.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.31\textwidth}
                >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.27\textwidth}
                >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.30\textwidth}}
\textbf{Topic here} & \textbf{Companion location} & \textbf{Status here}\\
\hline
Matching versus non-neutral components & Theorem 5.20 & Pullback-site
reformulation with the dependency chain displayed\\
Quotient initiality & Theorem 6.13 & Standard finite-nerve UCT clause in
\Cref{prop:uct-aggregate-package}\\
Component obstruction framework & Section 5 & Standard Giraud construction,
cited at theorem level\\
Terminal representative rigidity & No identical statement & Full narrow
no-go proof in \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity}\\
Finite-label prescribed realization & No identical package & Simultaneous
control theorem in \Cref{thm:prescribed-component-image-construction}\\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The table identifies overlap rather than claiming separate priority for the
first three rows.

\subsection*{Organization}

Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the minimal presheaf and prestack
interface.  Section~\ref{sec:gerbe-obstruction} records the standard Giraud
component package and the terminal torsor obstruction, records the
essentially surjective marked terminal form and its distinct pointed-atlas
alternative, proves the comparison criterion, and gives the full
terminal-rigidity proof.  Section~\ref{sec:homological-visibility} proves the
coherently trivialized connected-overlap, basis-site, and derived comparisons
before constructing the prescribed finite-label prestack from supplied
classes on a fixed cover and band.  Section~\ref{sec:homological-images}
collects the UCT and aggregate consequences.  The wedge application and the
empirical-model boundary occupy Sections~\ref{sec:wedge-application} and
\ref{sec:empirical-boundary}.  The separately compiled technical appendix
contains only presentation bookkeeping, extended examples, and the narrow
lower-language boundary argument; the proofs needed to certify the principal
claims are all contained here.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The article starts with supplied finite-site data: a presheaf, an
abelian-banded prestack lift, and its stackification.  Giraud's component
construction then assigns the maximal component gerbe to each global section
of the component sheaf.  The use made of this standard input is narrow: under
slice separatedness and terminal essential surjectivity it compares the
strict presheaf predicate of matching without amalgamation with non-neutrality
of every global component.  Representative-rigidity shows why a strictly
pullback-stable choice of lift representatives is too restrictive in the
basic \(H^1\)-vanishing regime.

More sharply, stackification of a prestack is fully faithful.  Essential
surjectivity on a neutral terminal component therefore gives an equivalence
with the full neutral gerbe, whose object classes form an \(H^1\)-torsor and
whose object automorphisms are \(H^0\).  The marked terminal statement in
\Cref{thm:marked-terminal-torsor-form} retains those unavoidable ambiguities;
the pointed-atlas alternative of
\Cref{rem:pointed-atlas-terminal-form} is recorded separately and is not
combined with it.  These are sharp structural consequences of standard
torsor theory, not a presentation-localization result.

On a finite good-cover site, connected overlaps together with coherent
trivializations that identify every coefficient group with one fixed \(A\)
and every restriction map with \(\operatorname{id}_A\) permit the ordinary
nerve to carry the full constant-coefficient Cech complex.  The
all-subdivision basis comparison identifies the generated site with the
ordinary sheaf theory of the underlying polyhedron.  Within this fixed
setting, the standard Cech-cocycle gerbe construction can be packaged into a
single prestack whose component presheaf, terminal behavior, neutrality
pattern, and evaluation images are prescribed simultaneously.

UCT and elementary subgroup arithmetic then yield the aggregate quotients.
For the selected open-star covers of
\(\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2\), the two-component realization criterion is
\[
 d(G)\le2\beta
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 G\text{ is not cyclic of prime-power order}.
\]
This is a sharp corollary of the selected realization, not a new
classification principle for finite abelian groups or gerbes.

Bare empirical models provide only the support presheaf and its canonical
split stack, whose component gerbes are neutral.  Their relative degree-one
obstructions are indexed differently and are not recovered by the
component-section map.  A non-split banded lift must therefore be supplied
before the finite-site results apply.

The resulting contribution has a definite boundary.  The following parts
are classical inputs:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{component over }v\text{ is a gerbe}
 &\text{Giraud III.2.1.5.3},\\
\text{neutrality}\Longleftrightarrow[\mathfrak G_v]=0
 &\text{abelian-banded gerbe classification},\\
\text{finite Cech class}\longrightarrow\text{UCT evaluation}
 &\text{Leray comparison and UCT},\\
\text{aggregate exact sequence}
 &\text{subgroup and quotient arithmetic.}
\end{array}
\]
They are stated together so that the hypotheses used by the applications
remain visible, not as separate advances.

The two proofs requiring construction beyond those inputs are terminal
rigidity and prescribed simultaneous realization.  The first identifies
where literal pullback stability removes a descent cocycle and where
\(H^1\)-vanishing removes the remaining Isom torsor.  The second constructs
the label presheaf and twisted groupoid fibres, verifies strict restrictions
and the genuine constant band, computes stackification components and
terminal objects, and recovers the selected Cech cocycles.  Their full proofs
make the claimed scope independently checkable within the article.

The technical appendix has a limited role.  Its presentation groupoid records
naturality only along specified comparison words and does not assert path
independence.  Its finite computations illustrate the UCT and subgroup
formulas.  Its lower-language example explains why the finite-site lift is
treated as input but does not construct that lift.

A genuinely presentation-independent theorem would require localization over
common refinements, including independence of refinement maps and zigzags and
the proof that the resulting cocycle-to-gerbe \(2\)-functor is a
biequivalence.  That full localization, rather than the terminal structural
statements above, is the substantive result not supplied by the present
article.

No crossed-module comparison is pursued: the present arguments begin after a
gerbe \(H^2\)-class and its Cech representative are supplied, and contain
neither the source-side degree-three chain model nor the comparison cochain
required to derive such a class from crossed-module data.

\title[Finite-Site Component Gerbes]{Finite-Site Component Gerbes and Homological Images}
\author{Haobo Ma}
\address[Haobo Ma]{AELF PTE LTD., \#14-02, Marina Bay Financial Centre Tower 1, 8 Marina Blvd, Singapore 018981}
\email[Haobo Ma]{auric@aelf.io}

\address[Wenlin Zhang]{National University of Singapore, Singapore}
\email[Wenlin Zhang]{e1327962@u.nus.edu}

\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
For a stack, Giraud's component construction identifies the full substack
over a global component section as its maximal component gerbe.  We apply
this standard construction to a banded prestack lift of a presheaf on a
finite site.  Under slice separatedness and terminal essential surjectivity,
matching without amalgamation is equivalent to non-neutrality of every
global component gerbe.  A representative-rigidity theorem shows that a
strictly pullback-stable choice of lift representatives forces terminal
effectivity when the band has vanishing first cohomology.  Terminal essential
surjectivity identifies each neutral source fibre with the full torsor
groupoid: its isomorphism classes form an \(H^1\)-torsor and its stabilizers
are \(H^0\).  Thus a singleton neutral source fibre forces \(H^1=0\).  On a
  fixed finite good cover with connected nonempty intersections, coherent
  trivializations to one fixed finite coefficient group $A$ and its constant
  band, and
  $H_1(N,\mathbb Z)=0$, we give a self-contained, object-level Cech-cocycle
  prestack construction simultaneously controlling the component presheaf,
  terminal fibre, neutral labels, and supplied gerbe classes, equivalently
  their prescribed evaluation maps $H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A$.  UCT and elementary
subgroup arithmetic yield the aggregate quotients.  For the selected
open-star sites of $\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2$, a nonzero finite abelian group
$G$ occurs as the two-component comparison kernel with complementary nonzero
images exactly when $d(G)\le2\beta$ and $G$ is not cyclic of prime-power
order.  This is a realization corollary for supplied lift data and does not
transfer to bare empirical models.
\end{abstract}

# Literature and Priority Check

Date of record: 15 August 2026 (Asia/Singapore).

## Scope and evidentiary basis

This record states the priority boundary supported by the current manuscript,
its `references.bib`, and the external assessment in
`oracle_sprint_A9_referee.md`. It is not a claim that an exhaustive literature
search can certify absolute priority. In particular, a statement not found
verbatim in the referee's targeted search is not thereby a substantial new
mathematical result.

All bibliographic metadata asserted below were checked against
`references.bib`. Chapter and proposition locators were also checked against
the citations in the manuscript. No unconfirmed bibliographic detail is used.

## Direct antecedent: Giraud's component-gerbe construction

The relevant book is Jean Giraud, *Cohomologie non abelienne*, Grundlehren der
mathematischen Wissenschaften 179, Springer-Verlag, 1971. These metadata are
the metadata recorded in `references.bib`.

Chapter III, Proposition 2.1.5.3 is the direct antecedent for the
component-gerbe construction. For any stack `S`, the projection

```text
S -> pi_0(S)
```

makes `S` a gerbe over its sheaf of connected components, and pullback along a
section of `pi_0(S)` gives the corresponding maximal subgerbe. As the referee
observes, this is essentially the structural content of Theorems 4.8(i) and
4.9. It is an input to this paper, not a contribution of this paper. The map
that assigns the gerbe class of the component selected by a section is useful
packaging for later comparisons, but it is not a new construction principle.

The paper also cites Giraud, Chapter IV for the classification of
abelian-banded gerbes by `H^2`, including the identification of neutral gerbes
with the zero class. That classification is a different result from the
Chapter III component-gerbe construction. Both results are used here, and
both are prior work.

## Standard inputs and formal consequences

The referee's assessment is that much of the advertised theorem structure is
textbook gerbe theory, universal-coefficient-theorem naturality, finite
duality, subgroup arithmetic, or fibre counting. The exact organization may
be specific to this manuscript, but the mathematical advance is smaller than
the theorem count and theorem-level presentation suggest.

The following boundaries therefore apply.

| Material used in the paper | Priority status |
|---|---|
| A component selected by a global component section is a maximal subgerbe | Giraud, Chapter III, Proposition 2.1.5.3; standard input |
| Neutrality is equivalent to existence of a global object, and abelian-banded gerbes are classified by `H^2` | Giraud, Chapter IV; standard input |
| Local objects, overlap arrows, triple-overlap Cech 2-cocycles, and change of representative by a coboundary | Standard gerbe theory |
| Realization of a supplied `H^2` class by an abelian-band gerbe | Standard gerbe theory |
| The matching/non-neutrality equivalence | A paper-specific corollary obtained by matching separatedness, sheafification, terminal essential surjectivity, and neutrality; not a new gerbe obstruction theorem, and substantially present in the cited companion project |
| Homological images, Ext-kernel descriptions, annihilating-character descriptions, and quotient factorization | Formal consequences of UCT naturality, finite duality, and quotient universal properties |
| Intersection/sum quotients and their exact sequence | Elementary subgroup and quotient arithmetic |
| Unrestricted auxiliary-register sizes | Fibre cardinality of quotient maps, not an independent information-theoretic result |
| The finite-abelian decomposition used in the wedge result | Standard finite-abelian group structure and generator arithmetic |
| The split component stack used in the empirical-model comparison | Standard construction |

Accordingly, whenever this manuscript applies one of these facts in its chosen
finite-site notation, that application should be described as an application
of a standard result. New notation, a named quotient, or a theorem-sized
restatement does not by itself establish mathematical priority.

## Two-label wedge classification

The referee found no previously published theorem stating the entire
two-label wedge classification verbatim. That negative search result must be
recorded together with its qualification: it does not support a substantial
priority claim. An exact statement obtained by composing standard
equivalences can be formally new while carrying little independent
mathematical priority.

Here the wedge statement is derived from `H_2` of a wedge of 2-spheres, the
description of attainable images of maps from a free abelian group, the
equivalence between complementary image subgroups and an internal direct-sum
decomposition, the classification of finite indecomposable abelian groups,
and generator bounds on the two summands. The resulting exact criterion may
be specific to this selected realization problem, but it is an elementary
two-component realization corollary, not a new classification theorem about
finite abelian groups or gerbes. It is also presentation-relative to the
chosen good-cover construction.

## Closed route: Neeb-Wagemann-Wockel comparison

The bibliography records Karl-Hermann Neeb, Friedrich Wagemann, and Christoph
Wockel, *Making Lifting Obstructions Explicit*, Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society 106(3) (2013), 589--620, DOI
`10.1112/plms/pds047`, arXiv:`1108.5853`.

The crossed-module comparison discussed in connection with that work is an
explicitly closed route for this paper. This paper begins only after a gerbe
`H^2` class and a Cech representative of that class have been supplied. It
does not contain the source-side degree-three locally continuous or locally
smooth group-cohomology chain model, the characteristic 3-cocycle derived
from strict crossed-module data, or the comparison cochain needed to identify
its Cechization with the lifting-gerbe 2-cocycle.

In particular, the missing step is not supplied by the paper's UCT images,
finite quotients, banded-equivalence naturality, or wedge calculation. It
would require an explicit cochain comparison, with conventions, choice
independence, refinement compatibility, and naturality proved at chain level.
The current paper therefore neither derives a gerbe class from crossed-module
data nor claims to solve that comparison problem. Pursuing the comparison
would require a separate source-side theory and a separate proof, not an
extension of the results recorded here.

## Defensible paper-specific remainder

After the prior inputs and formal consequences above are removed from the
priority account, the defensible paper-specific content is narrow:

1. The exact representative-rigid terminal-fibre no-go formulation is the
   strongest plausible technical priority claim identified by the referee.
   Its formulation may be new, but its ingredients - split cleavages,
   pseudofunctorial pullback choices, and `H^1` classification of torsors -
   are classical. It is not a new general descent principle.

2. The exact prestack presentation simultaneously controls the component
   presheaf, terminal essential surjectivity, neutral versus non-neutral
   labels, and prescribed componentwise homological images, and places these
   controls inside the paper's typed-model convention. This simultaneous
   finite-label/presheaf packaging is paper-specific. The underlying
   Cech-cocycle gerbe realization and the disjoint-union assembly are standard
   inputs.

3. The exact two-label wedge criterion is, at most, a sharp algebraic
   corollary for the selected realization construction. The referee found no
   verbatim antecedent, but this supports only a claim about the exact
   packaging, not a substantial independent classification priority.

4. The empty-domain comparison with local-section-indexed contextuality
   classes is a useful narrow boundary observation: for a strongly contextual
   empirical model there is no global component section, while the comparison
   classes are indexed by local sections. The split stack used to expose this
   mismatch is standard.

5. The one-model, one-variable, parameter-free, constant-free lower-language
   separation example is plausibly specific to the paper but deliberately
   narrow. It does not establish general expressive incomparability.

The organization of presentation-relative homological images is bookkeeping
that may be useful to readers, not an independent priority claim. The
referee also identified unresolved overlap with an unpublished companion
manuscript for the component-obstruction framework, the matching/non-neutral
criterion, and quotient initiality. Until that overlap is documented in a
theorem-by-theorem public comparison, chronological priority for those parts
cannot be certified here.

This is the priority boundary for the submission package: standard inputs are
credited as standard, exact packaging is not inflated into a broad novelty
claim, and the remaining claims are limited to the concrete formulations and
simultaneous controls listed above.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The article starts with supplied finite-site data: a presheaf, an
abelian-banded prestack lift, and its stackification.  Giraud's component
construction then assigns the maximal component gerbe to each global section
of the component sheaf.  The use made of this standard input is narrow: under
slice separatedness and terminal essential surjectivity it compares the
strict presheaf predicate of matching without amalgamation with non-neutrality
of every global component.  Representative-rigidity shows why a strictly
pullback-stable choice of lift representatives is too restrictive in the
basic \(H^1\)-vanishing regime.

More sharply, stackification of a prestack is fully faithful.  Essential
surjectivity on a neutral terminal component therefore gives an equivalence
with the full neutral gerbe, whose object classes form an \(H^1\)-torsor and
whose object automorphisms are \(H^0\).  The marked terminal statement in
\Cref{thm:marked-terminal-torsor-form} retains those unavoidable ambiguities;
the pointed-atlas alternative of
\Cref{rem:pointed-atlas-terminal-form} is recorded separately and is not
combined with it.  These are sharp structural consequences of standard
torsor theory, not a presentation-localization result.

On a finite good-cover site, connected overlaps together with coherent
trivializations that identify every coefficient group with one fixed \(A\)
and every restriction map with \(\operatorname{id}_A\) permit the ordinary
nerve to carry the full constant-coefficient Cech complex.  The
all-subdivision basis comparison identifies the generated site with the
ordinary sheaf theory of the underlying polyhedron.  Within this fixed
setting, the standard Cech-cocycle gerbe construction can be packaged into a
single prestack whose component presheaf, terminal behavior, neutrality
pattern, and evaluation images are prescribed simultaneously.

UCT and elementary subgroup arithmetic then yield the aggregate quotients.
For the selected open-star covers of
\(\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2\), the two-component realization criterion is
\[
 d(G)\le2\beta
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 G\text{ is not cyclic of prime-power order}.
\]
This is a sharp corollary of the selected realization, not a new
classification principle for finite abelian groups or gerbes.

Bare empirical models provide only the support presheaf and its canonical
split stack, whose component gerbes are neutral.  Their relative degree-one
obstructions are indexed differently and are not recovered by the
component-section map.  A non-split banded lift must therefore be supplied
before the finite-site results apply.

The resulting contribution has a definite boundary.  The following parts
are classical inputs:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{component over }v\text{ is a gerbe}
 &\text{Giraud III.2.1.5.3},\\
\text{neutrality}\Longleftrightarrow[\mathfrak G_v]=0
 &\text{abelian-banded gerbe classification},\\
\text{finite Cech class}\longrightarrow\text{UCT evaluation}
 &\text{Leray comparison and UCT},\\
\text{aggregate exact sequence}
 &\text{subgroup and quotient arithmetic.}
\end{array}
\]
They are stated together so that the hypotheses used by the applications
remain visible, not as separate advances.

The two proofs requiring construction beyond those inputs are terminal
rigidity and prescribed simultaneous realization.  The first identifies
where literal pullback stability removes a descent cocycle and where
\(H^1\)-vanishing removes the remaining Isom torsor.  The second constructs
the label presheaf and twisted groupoid fibres, verifies strict restrictions
and the genuine constant band, computes stackification components and
terminal objects, and recovers the selected Cech cocycles.  Their full proofs
make the claimed scope independently checkable within the article.

The technical appendix has a limited role.  Its presentation groupoid records
naturality only along specified comparison words and does not assert path
independence.  Its finite computations illustrate the UCT and subgroup
formulas.  Its lower-language example explains why the finite-site lift is
treated as input but does not construct that lift.

A genuinely presentation-independent theorem would require localization over
common refinements, including independence of refinement maps and zigzags and
the proof that the resulting cocycle-to-gerbe \(2\)-functor is a
biequivalence.  That full localization, rather than the terminal structural
statements above, is the substantive result not supplied by the present
article.

No crossed-module comparison is pursued: the present arguments begin after a
gerbe \(H^2\)-class and its Cech representative are supplied, and contain
neither the source-side degree-three chain model nor the comparison cochain
required to derive such a class from crossed-module data.

search can certify absolute priority. In particular, a statement not found
verbatim in the referee's targeted search is not thereby a substantial new
mathematical result.

All bibliographic metadata asserted below were checked against
`references.bib`. Chapter and proposition locators were also checked against
the citations in the manuscript. No unconfirmed bibliographic detail is used.

## Direct antecedent: Giraud's component-gerbe construction

The relevant book is Jean Giraud, *Cohomologie non abelienne*, Grundlehren der
mathematischen Wissenschaften 179, Springer-Verlag, 1971. These metadata are
the metadata recorded in `references.bib`.

Chapter III, Proposition 2.1.5.3 is the direct antecedent for the
component-gerbe construction. For any stack `S`, the projection

```text
S -> pi_0(S)
```

makes `S` a gerbe over its sheaf of connected components, and pullback along a
section of `pi_0(S)` gives the corresponding maximal subgerbe. As the referee
observes, this is essentially the structural content of Theorems 4.8(i) and
4.9. It is an input to this paper, not a contribution of this paper. The map
that assigns the gerbe class of the component selected by a section is useful
packaging for later comparisons, but it is not a new construction principle.

The paper also cites Giraud, Chapter IV for the classification of
abelian-banded gerbes by `H^2`, including the identification of neutral gerbes
with the zero class. That classification is a different result from the
Chapter III component-gerbe construction. Both results are used here, and
both are prior work.

## Standard inputs and formal consequences

The referee's assessment is that much of the advertised theorem structure is
textbook gerbe theory, universal-coefficient-theorem naturality, finite
duality, subgroup arithmetic, or fibre counting. The exact organization may
be specific to this manuscript, but the mathematical advance is smaller than
the theorem count and theorem-level presentation suggest.

The following boundaries therefore apply.

| Material used in the paper | Priority status |
|---|---|
| A component selected by a global component section is a maximal subgerbe | Giraud, Chapter III, Proposition 2.1.5.3; standard input |
| Neutrality is equivalent to existence of a global object, and abelian-banded gerbes are classified by `H^2` | Giraud, Chapter IV; standard input |
| Local objects, overlap arrows, triple-overlap Cech 2-cocycles, and change of representative by a coboundary | Standard gerbe theory |
| Realization of a supplied `H^2` class by an abelian-band gerbe | Standard gerbe theory |
| The matching/non-neutrality equivalence | A paper-specific corollary obtained by matching separatedness, sheafification, terminal essential surjectivity, and neutrality; not a new gerbe obstruction theorem, and substantially present in the cited companion project |
| Homological images, Ext-kernel descriptions, annihilating-character descriptions, and quotient factorization | Formal consequences of UCT naturality, finite duality, and quotient universal properties |
| Intersection/sum quotients and their exact sequence | Elementary subgroup and quotient arithmetic |
| Unrestricted auxiliary-register sizes | Fibre cardinality of quotient maps, not an independent information-theoretic result |
| The finite-abelian decomposition used in the wedge result | Standard finite-abelian group structure and generator arithmetic |
| The split component stack used in the empirical-model comparison | Standard construction |

Accordingly, whenever this manuscript applies one of these facts in its chosen
finite-site notation, that application should be described as an application
of a standard result. New notation, a named quotient, or a theorem-sized
restatement does not by itself establish mathematical priority.

## Two-label wedge classification

The referee found no previously published theorem stating the entire
two-label wedge classification verbatim. That negative search result must be
recorded together with its qualification: it does not support a substantial
priority claim. An exact statement obtained by composing standard
equivalences can be formally new while carrying little independent
mathematical priority.

Here the wedge statement is derived from `H_2` of a wedge of 2-spheres, the
description of attainable images of maps from a free abelian group, the
equivalence between complementary image subgroups and an internal direct-sum
decomposition, the classification of finite indecomposable abelian groups,
and generator bounds on the two summands. The resulting exact criterion may
be specific to this selected realization problem, but it is an elementary
two-component realization corollary, not a new classification theorem about
finite abelian groups or gerbes. It is also presentation-relative to the
chosen good-cover construction.

## Closed route: Neeb-Wagemann-Wockel comparison

The bibliography records Karl-Hermann Neeb, Friedrich Wagemann, and Christoph
Wockel, *Making Lifting Obstructions Explicit*, Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society 106(3) (2013), 589--620, DOI
`10.1112/plms/pds047`, arXiv:`1108.5853`.

The crossed-module comparison discussed in connection with that work is an
explicitly closed route for this paper. This paper begins only after a gerbe
`H^2` class and a Cech representative of that class have been supplied. It
does not contain the source-side degree-three locally continuous or locally
smooth group-cohomology chain model, the characteristic 3-cocycle derived
from strict crossed-module data, or the comparison cochain needed to identify
its Cechization with the lifting-gerbe 2-cocycle.

In particular, the missing step is not supplied by the paper's UCT images,
finite quotients, banded-equivalence naturality, or wedge calculation. It
would require an explicit cochain comparison, with conventions, choice
independence, refinement compatibility, and naturality proved at chain level.
The current paper therefore neither derives a gerbe class from crossed-module
data nor claims to solve that comparison problem. Pursuing the comparison
would require a separate source-side theory and a separate proof, not an
extension of the results recorded here.

## Defensible paper-specific remainder

After the prior inputs and formal consequences above are removed from the
priority account, the defensible paper-specific content is narrow:

1. The exact representative-rigid terminal-fibre no-go formulation is the
   strongest plausible technical priority claim identified by the referee.
   Its formulation may be new, but its ingredients - split cleavages,
   pseudofunctorial pullback choices, and `H^1` classification of torsors -
   are classical. It is not a new general descent principle.

2. The exact prestack presentation simultaneously controls the component
   presheaf, terminal essential surjectivity, neutral versus non-neutral
   labels, and prescribed componentwise homological images, and places these
   controls inside the paper's typed-model convention. This simultaneous
   finite-label/presheaf packaging is paper-specific. The underlying
   Cech-cocycle gerbe realization and the disjoint-union assembly are standard
   inputs.

3. The exact two-label wedge criterion is, at most, a sharp algebraic
   corollary for the selected realization construction. The referee found no
   verbatim antecedent, but this supports only a claim about the exact
   packaging, not a substantial independent classification priority.

4. The empty-domain comparison with local-section-indexed contextuality
   classes is a useful narrow boundary observation: for a strongly contextual
   empirical model there is no global component section, while the comparison
   classes are indexed by local sections. The split stack used to expose this
   mismatch is standard.

5. The one-model, one-variable, parameter-free, constant-free lower-language
   separation example is plausibly specific to the paper but deliberately
   narrow. It does not establish general expressive incomparability.

The organization of presentation-relative homological images is bookkeeping
that may be useful to readers, not an independent priority claim. The
referee also identified unresolved overlap with an unpublished companion
manuscript for the component-obstruction framework, the matching/non-neutral
criterion, and quotient initiality. Until that overlap is documented in a
theorem-by-theorem public comparison, chronological priority for those parts
cannot be certified here.

This is the priority boundary for the submission package: standard inputs are
credited as standard, exact packaging is not inflated into a broad novelty
claim, and the remaining claims are limited to the concrete formulations and
simultaneous controls listed above.

    <summary>We establish a strong link between two apparently unrelated topics: the study of conflicting information in the formal framework of valuation algebras, and the phenomena of non-locality and contextuality. In particular, we show that these peculiar features of quantum theory are mathematically equivalent to a general notion of \emph{disagreement} between information sources. This result vastly generalises previously observed connections between contextuality, relational databases, constraint satisfaction problems, and logical paradoxes, and gives further proof that contextual behaviour is not a phenomenon limited to quantum physics, but pervades various domains of mathematics and computer science. The connection allows to translate theorems, methods and algorithms from one field to the other, and paves the way for the application of generic inference algorithms to study contextuality.</summary>

    <summary>An important class of contextuality arguments in quantum foundations are the All-versus-Nothing (AvN) proofs, generalising a construction originally due to Mermin. We present a general formulation of All-versus-Nothing arguments, and a complete characterisation of all such arguments which arise from stabiliser states. We show that every AvN argument for an n-qubit stabiliser state can be reduced to an AvN proof for a three-qubit state which is local Clifford-equivalent to the tripartite GHZ state. This is achieved through a combinatorial characterisation of AvN arguments, the AvN triple Theorem, whose proof makes use of the theory of graph states. This result enables the development of a computational method to generate all the AvN arguments in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ on n-qubit stabiliser states. We also present new insights into the stabiliser formalism and its connections with logic.</summary>

    <title>Minimum quantum resources for strong non-locality</title>
    <updated>2017-05-25T18:08:34Z</updated>

    <summary>We analyse the minimum quantum resources needed to realise strong non-locality, as exemplified e.g. by the classical GHZ construction. It was already known that no two-qubit system, with any finite number of local measurements, can realise strong non-locality. For three-qubit systems, we show that strong non-locality can only be realised in the GHZ SLOCC class, and with equatorial measurements. However, we show that in this class there is an infinite family of states which are pairwise non-LU-equivalent that realise strong non-locality with finitely many measurements. These states have decreasing entanglement between one qubit and the other two, necessitating an increasing number of local measurements on the latter.</summary>

    <updated>2017-01-03T11:14:35Z</updated>

    <summary>Recent work by Abramsky and Brandenburger used sheaf theory to give a mathematical formulation of non-locality and contextuality. By adopting this viewpoint, it has been possible to define cohomological obstructions to the existence of global sections.     <title>Topological proofs of contextuality in quantum mechanics</title>
    <updated>2017-10-17T02:49:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.01888v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.01888v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We provide a cohomological framework for contextuality of quantum mechanics that is suited to describing contextuality as a resource in measurement-based quantum computation. This framework applies to the parity proofs first discussed by Mermin, as well as a different type of contextuality proofs based on symmetry transformations. The topological arguments presented can be used in the state-dependent and the state-independent case.</summary>

31-using C ech cohomology [4, 2, 7].

36-of the Pauli measurements used in MBQC. We give a more abstract account of this approach using the

599-
600-We have considered two different applications of cohomological techniques to contextuality in MBQC.
601-While the C ech cohomology obstruction is defined for any set of quantum measurements, the group
602-cohomology obstruction relies on the specific algebraic structure of the Pauli measurements. We have
603-given an abstract account of this approach using the sheaf theoretic framework. At this level of generality
604-we observe that although both approaches rely on structural assumptions to be complete, there is a direct
605:way in which the C ech cohomology obstruction subsumes the group cohomology obstruction.
606-
607-    Our presentation of the group cohomology approach deviates from Okay et al.'s in that we have
608-defined a single obstruction that applies to both state independent and state dependent contextuality. We
609-have shown that this obstruction detects contextuality in the state independent case of Mermin's square
610-and the state dependent case of GHZ.

10-
11-        Recent work by Abramsky and Brandenburger used sheaf theory to give a mathematical formulation
12-        of non-locality and contextuality. By adopting this viewpoint, it has been possible to define cohomo-
13-        logical obstructions to the existence of global sections. In the present work, we illustrate new insights
14-        into different aspects of this theory. We shed light on the power of detection of the cohomological
15:        obstruction by showing that it is not a complete invariant for strong contextuality even under symme-
16:        try and connectedness restrictions on the measurement cover, disproving a previous conjecture. We
17:        generalise obstructions to higher cohomology groups and show that they give rise to a refinement of
18-        the notion of cohomological contextuality: different "levels" of contextuality are organised in a hier-
19-        archy of logical implications. Finally, we present an alternative description of the first cohomology
20-        group in terms of torsors, resulting in a new interpretation of the cohomological obstructions.

39-evidence of a restricted number of false positives (e.g. the Hardy model [15]).

41-    In the present paper, we illustrate new insights into the properties of cohomological obstructions
42-with the ultimate goal of understanding how such false positives arise. In particular, we aim to give
43-an answer to some of the open questions left by [5]: "Is the cohomological obstruction a full invari-
44:ant for strong contextuality under suitable restrictions on the measurement scenario?"; "Can higher
45-cohomology groups be used for the study of contextuality?"; "Is there a concrete way of describing
46-cohomological obstructions?".

53-    We briefly outline our results:
54-
55-    ? We disprove Conjecture 8.1 of [5] by providing an explicit example of a strongly contextual but
56-       cohomologically non-contextual empirical model defined on a simple (2, 2, 4) Bell-type scenario
57:       which verifies any reasonably strong form of connectedness and symmetry condition.
58-
59:    ? We generalise cohomological obstructions to higher cohomology groups. It turns out that this
60:       procedure can be done in a natural way only in odd dimensions. We obtain a refinement of the
61-       notion of cohomological contextuality: for each q  0, we say that a model is q-cohomologically
62:       contextual if the q-th obstruction does not vanish.
63-
64:    ? We show that higher obstructions are organised in a precise hierarchy of logical implications.
65-       We also prove that, unfortunately, this result cannot be used in the study of contextuality in no-
66:       signalling empirical models. Despite this fact, higher obstructions could potentially be used to
67-       study signalling properties.
68-
69-    ? We give a new description of the first cohomology group (thus, in particular, of the cohomology
70-       obstructions) using torsors relative to a presheaf.
71-
72-    The paper is organised as follows. We summarise the sheaf viewpoint from [3] in Section 2, and recall
73:the main definitions concerning sheaf cohomology in Section 3. Section 4 features the counterexample
74:to Conjecture 8.1 of [5]. We generalise cohomological obstructions to higher cohomology groups in
75-Section 5. Finally, in Section 6, we present torsors relative to a presheaf, and their relation to the first
76-sheaf cohomology group.

342:4 A false positive for strong contextuality
343-
344-In [5], it is brought to attention that, although cohomology can fail to detect logical contextuality as in
345-the case of the Hardy model, it is rather difficult to construct a strongly contextual false positive. Indeed,
346:cohomology is able to detect the strong contextuality of a variety of well-known models, including GHZ
347-states [12, 13, 20], PR Boxes [25], the Peres-Mermin "magic" square [22, 21, 24], all ?GCD models [5],
348-and the whole class of models admitting All-vs-Nothing arguments [2]. The only known example of a
349-strongly contextual false positive is the Kochen-Specker model [17, 19] for the cover
350-
351-                       {A, B,C}, {B, D, E}, {C, D, E}, {A, D, F}, {A, E, G},
352-
353:which "does not satisfy any reasonable criterion for symmetry, nor does it satisfy any strong form of
354:connectedness" and where "the existence of measurements belonging to a single context, namely F and
355-G, seems to be crucial" [5]. Due to these limitations, the following conjecture was made:
356-
357:Conjecture 4.1 (Conjecture 8.1 of [5]). Under suitable assumptions of symmetry and connectedness of
358:the cover, the cohomology obstruction is a complete invariant for strong contextuality.
359-
360:    In Figure 4, we introduce a counterexample to this conjecture.

542-6 An alternative description of the first cohomology group
543-
544:Since higher cohomology groups cannot be used to infer information on how false positives arise, we
545-devote the last section of this paper to a detailed study of the first cohomology group H 1(M , FC~0). As
546-explained in [5], this group is of crucial importance for the cohomological study of contextuality, as it
547-contains all of the obstructions to the existence of global sections. Its relevance has been also previously
548-highlighted by Penrose in his On the cohomology of impossible figures [23], which presents "intriguing
549-resemblances" with our study [2]. Yet a full grasp of the nature of its elements is still to be achieved. We
--

645-trivial F -torsor will be simply denoted by F .

647-
648:for contextuality (neither logical nor strong) even under reasonably strong assumptions on symmetry and
649:connectedness of the cover, and, although obstructions can be generalised to higher cohomology groups,
650:they cannot be applied to the study of no-signalling empirical models. In future work, we aim to re-
651-develop the sheaf-cohomological study of contextuality from a different viewpoint. The machinery of
652-obstruction theory, a branch of homotopy theory that deals with the extendability of maps, allows the def-
653-inition of obstructions to the extension of continuous functions in a cohomology theory with coefficients
654-in the homotopy groups. This promising approach will require an adaptation of the concept of empiri-
655-cal model to fit this framework. A possibility would be to formalise the bundle diagram representation
